lessons.title: Types of mixers: batch, continuous, inline
lessons.body:
When you start making detergents, you need to choose how you will mix your ingredients. The three main types are batch, continuous, and inline mixers. Each has its place in a small African workshop.

Batch mixing is the simplest. You measure all your ingredients, put them in a tank, and mix until uniform. Then you stop and empty the tank. For example, to make 200 litres of liquid dishwash, you fill a 250-litre plastic drum with 150 litres of water, add 20 kg of sulphonic acid slowly while stirring, then add caustic soda solution until the pH is 7-8, then add salt and fragrance. You mix for 30-45 minutes with a paddle or electric drill with a mixing attachment. Batch mixing is good for small-scale production, say up to 500 litres per day. It is easy to control quality because you can test each batch.

Continuous mixing means ingredients flow into one end of a mixer and product flows out the other end non-stop. This is used in big factories making thousands of litres per hour. You need pumps, flow meters, and automatic controls. For a beginner, continuous mixing is too expensive and complicated. But you can see it in large soap and detergent plants.

Inline mixing is when you mix as the product moves through a pipe. For example, you can use a static mixerâa pipe with twisted blades insideâto blend a liquid detergent with a fragrance just before filling bottles. Inline mixers are cheap and have no moving parts. They work well when you already have a liquid stream and want to add a small amount of another liquid. You can buy a static mixer for under $100.

For most small African businesses, batch mixing is the best starting point. You can use a 200-litre drum, a heavy-duty drill with a paint mixer attachment, and a weighing scale. As you grow, you might add an inline mixer for adding perfume. Continuous mixing only makes sense when you produce more than 5,000 litres per day. So start with batch, master it, and then consider other types when your sales demand it.

lessons.title: Order of ingredient addition
lessons.body:
The order in which you add ingredients can make the difference between a perfect batch and a ruined one. In detergent making, always follow this rule: start with the hardest-to-dissolve ingredients and end with the easiest. Also, never add concentrated acid to concentrated causticâthat can cause a violent reaction.

For a typical liquid detergent like dishwash, begin with water. Fill your mixing tank about 70% full with clean water. If you use borehole water, let it settle or filter it first. Then add the acid, such as sulphonic acid or LABSA. Pour it slowly while stirring. The acid is thick and needs time to dissolve. Stir for 10-15 minutes until no lumps remain. Next, add the caustic soda solution (sodium hydroxide dissolved in water) very slowly. This neutralises the acid and creates the detergent. Watch the temperatureâit will rise. If it gets above 60Â°C, stop adding caustic and wait for it to cool. Stir for another 15 minutes.

After neutralisation, add builders like sodium carbonate or sodium silicate. These help soften water and improve cleaning. Add them slowly to avoid clumping. Then add foam boosters like coco diethanolamide (CDEA) or lauryl sulphate. These are thick and sticky, so mix well. Next, add salt (sodium chloride) to thicken the mixture. Add a small amount at a timeâtoo much salt will thin it instead. Finally, add fragrance, colour, and preservative. These are sensitive to heat, so add them when the mixture is below 40Â°C.

For powdered detergents, the order is different: first mix dry powders like soda ash, STPP, and sodium sulphate. Then add surfactants that are already in powder form (like sodium lauryl sulphate powder). Finally, spray or mix in liquid ingredients like fragrance and nonionic surfactants. Always add liquids last to avoid caking.

Remember: never add water to acid; always add acid to water. And always add caustic to water, not water to caustic. Following the correct order prevents accidents and ensures a smooth, stable product.

lessons.title: Mixing parameters: speed, time, temperature
lessons.body:
To get consistent quality, you must control three key mixing parameters: speed, time, and temperature. If you ignore any of these, your detergent may be lumpy, too thin, too thick, or unstable.

Speed: The speed of your mixer depends on what you are mixing. For dissolving powders in water, use a medium speedâabout 300 to 600 RPM (revolutions per minute). A standard electric drill with a paddle mixer runs at about 500-800 RPM. If you mix too fast, you create foam and air bubbles that are hard to remove. If you mix too slow, powders settle at the bottom. For emulsification (mixing oil and water), you need higher speed, around 1,500 to 3,000 RPM. You can use a high-shear mixer or a blender for small batches. For thickening with salt, use low speed (100-200 RPM) to avoid thinning the mixture.

Time: Each step has a minimum mixing time. For acid dissolution, mix for at least 15 minutes. For neutralisation, mix for 20 minutes after adding caustic. For salt thickening, mix for 10 minutes, then check viscosity. Over-mixing can also be a problemâit can break down foam or cause excessive aeration. A good rule: mix until the mixture is uniform, then mix 5 more minutes. Use a timer.

Temperature: Most liquid detergents are made at room temperature (25-30Â°C). But neutralisation generates heat. Keep the temperature below 60Â°C. If it gets too hot, the fragrance may evaporate and the colour may fade. For powdered detergents, you may need to dry the mixture at 60-80Â°C, but that is after mixing. For emulsification, warming the oil phase to 70Â°C and the water phase to 70Â°C helps form a stable emulsion. Then cool slowly while stirring.

In Africa, ambient temperatures can be high, so you may need to cool your mixing tank with a water bath or add ice to the water jacket. Always use a thermometerâa simple digital one costs less than $10. Record the speed, time, and temperature for every batch so you can repeat good results.

lessons.title: Homogenization and emulsification
lessons.body:
Homogenization and emulsification are two processes that make your detergent look smooth and stay mixed. Without them, your product may separate into layersâoil on top, water on bottomâwhich customers will not buy.

Emulsification is mixing two liquids that don't normally mix, like oil and water. In detergents, you often need to emulsify fragrance oils, silicone antifoams, or plant oils. To make a stable emulsion, you need an emulsifierâa chemical that bridges oil and water. Common emulsifiers in detergents are nonionic surfactants like alcohol ethoxylates or fatty acid ethoxylates. The process: heat the oil phase to 70Â°C, heat the water phase to 70Â°C, then slowly pour the oil into the water while stirring at high speed (1,500-3,000 RPM). Stir for 15-20 minutes, then cool slowly while stirring. If you cool too fast, the emulsion may crack. A simple hand blender can work for 5-10 litre batches. For larger batches, use a high-shear mixer.

Homogenization is forcing the mixture through a narrow gap at high pressure to break oil droplets into tiny sizes. This makes the emulsion more stable and gives a smoother feel. A homogenizer is expensive, but you can achieve similar results with a high-speed mixer or a colloid mill. For small-scale production, a colloid mill (costing around $500-$1,000) can homogenize 100-500 litres per hour. You can also use a high-pressure pump if available.

In Africa, many small producers skip homogenization because of cost. But if you make liquid handwash or body wash, homogenization makes a big difference. You can start by using a good emulsifier and a high-speed mixer. Test your emulsion by leaving a sample in a bottle for 7 days. If it separates, you need more emulsifier or better mixing. Also, avoid adding salt before emulsificationâsalt can break the emulsion. Add salt after the emulsion is formed and cooled.

Remember: stable emulsions need the right emulsifier, the right temperature, and the right mixing speed. Practice with small batches until you get a product that stays mixed for months.

lessons.title: Monitoring and control of mixing
lessons.body:
Monitoring and control mean checking your mixing process while it is happening and making adjustments to keep the product on track. Without monitoring, you are guessing, and guessing leads to wasted batches.

What to monitor: First, check the appearance. Is the mixture uniform? Are there lumps or streaks? Use a glass rod or a clean stick to take a sample. Second, measure pH. For most liquid detergents, pH should be between 7 and 9. Use pH paper or a digital pH meter (costing $20-$50). Third, check viscosity. You can use a simple flow cup or a viscometer. A cheap method: time how long it takes for a fixed volume to flow through a funnel. Record the time and compare to your standard. Fourth, check temperature with a thermometer. Fifth, check foam height if your product is for handwashingâtoo little foam means poor quality.

How to control: If pH is too high, add a little more acid. If too low, add a little caustic. Add in small amounts and mix for 5 minutes before testing again. If viscosity is too low, add salt solution (25% salt in water) slowly. If too high, add water. If temperature is too high, reduce mixing speed or cool the tank. If you see lumps, increase mixing speed or mix longer.

Tools for monitoring: In a small African workshop, you need a thermometer, pH paper or meter, a weighing scale, a measuring jug, and a timer. A notebook to record every batch is essential. Write down the date, batch number, ingredients and amounts, mixing speed, time, temperature, pH, and viscosity. This helps you trace problems and repeat successes.

Automation: If you grow, you can add simple controls like a variable speed drive for your mixer, a temperature controller, and a pH controller. But start manually. Train your workers to check and record. A good practice is to have a checklist for each step: Did you add acid slowly? Did you check pH after neutralisation? Did you add fragrance after cooling? Sign off each step. This simple system prevents most mistakes.

lessons.title: Cleaning and changeover procedures
lessons.body:
Cleaning between batches is critical. Leftover detergent from a previous batch can contaminate the next one, causing wrong colour, wrong smell, or even chemical reactions. Changeover means switching from making one product to another, like from dishwash to handwash. Proper cleaning and changeover save you money and protect your reputation.

Cleaning steps: First, drain all leftover product from the tank, pipes, and mixer. You can save this as 'first rinse' and use it for the next batch of the same product if it is still good. Second, rinse with water. Use a hose or buckets. For sticky residues, use warm water (40-50Â°C). Third, scrub with a brush or sponge. Pay attention to corners, the mixer shaft, and the bottom of the tank. Fourth, use a cleaning solution. For detergent residues, a 2% caustic soda solution works well. For oily residues, use a detergent solution. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then scrub again. Fifth, rinse with clean water until the water runs clear and has no foam. Sixth, sanitise if needed. For products like handwash, use a dilute bleach solution (100 ppm chlorine) and rinse again. Finally, dry the equipment or let it air dry.

Changeover procedure: When switching from one product to another, follow a written procedure. For example, from dishwash to handwash: drain, rinse, clean with caustic, rinse, then rinse with a weak acid (like vinegar) to neutralise any caustic. Then rinse again. Check the last rinse water with pH paperâit should be neutral (pH 7). Then you can start the new batch. If the two products have very different colours or fragrances, you may need to disassemble the mixer and clean it manually.

In Africa, water can be scarce, so use water wisely. Use a high-pressure sprayer to reduce water use. Collect rinse water and reuse it for the first rinse of the next cleaning. Keep a cleaning log: date, product, who cleaned, and how long it took. Train your workers to clean immediately after each batchâdried detergent is harder to remove. A clean plant is a safe plant. Also, cleaning prevents pests and bacteria that can spoil your product. Make cleaning a habit, not an afterthought.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mixing and Blending Operations in Detergent Manufacturing

In Africa's fast-growing detergent sector â from Lagos to Nairobi to Durban â the mixing and blending stage is where raw materials become a sellable product. Whether you are producing powdered detergent, liquid dishwash, or a multi-purpose cleaner, your mixing operation determines product quality, batch consistency, production cost, and how quickly you can respond to customer orders. This practical reference gives you the operational parameters, tables, and checklists you need to run a reliable mixing floor.

Detergent manufacturing in Africa is dominated by small and medium enterprises (SMEs) serving local markets. Many operate with a single mixer and a small team. The difference between a profitable operation and one that loses money on rework, rejects, and downtime is usually not the equipment â it is the discipline of the mixing process. This module covers mixer selection, ingredient order, mixing parameters, homogenization, monitoring, and changeover procedures.

1. Types of Mixers: Batch, Continuous, Inline

Your choice of mixer depends on your product, volume, and capital. For most African SMEs, batch mixing is the starting point. Continuous and inline systems become viable as volume grows and you need consistent output with less labour.

Table 1: Mixer types compared for African detergent SME operations
Mixer type Best for Typical batch size / throughput Capital cost Labour & skill Changeover
Batch (ribbon blender, paddle, planetary) Powdered detergent, small liquid batches, multiple SKUs 50 kg â 2,000 kg per batch Low â medium (US$500 â US$15,000) Low; manual weighing and charging Easy; clean between batches
Continuous (screw conveyor, ploughshare, twin-shaft) High-volume powder, single formulation 500 kg â 10 t/hour High (US$20,000+) Medium; needs calibration and monitoring Difficult; long purge required
Inline (static mixer, rotor-stator, high-shear pump) Liquid detergents, dilution, emulsification Continuous flow, 1 â 20 mÂ³/hour Medium â high Medium; requires pump and flow control Moderate; flush with water

Source: Adapted from UNIDO, Detergent Manufacturing: A Guide for Small and Medium Enterprises (2010), and Kenya Association of Manufacturers SME processing guides.

Business tip: Start with a batch ribbon blender for powders and a stainless steel tank with a propeller or high-shear mixer for liquids. This keeps capital low and lets you produce multiple SKUs â washing powder, dishwash, bleach â on the same line. Upgrade to continuous or inline only when a single product line justifies the volume.

2. Order of Ingredient Addition

Adding ingredients in the wrong order causes lumps, poor dissolution, phase separation, and wasted raw materials. For liquid detergents, the standard order is: water â chelating agent â surfactant â builder â additives â fragrance â dye â preservative. For powders, the order is: builder â surfactant â filler â additives â fragrance.

3. Mixing Parameters: Speed, Time, Temperature

Mixing parameters are the levers you control to get consistent product. Record them for every batch and keep a log. The table below gives practical starting ranges for common detergent types in African SME conditions.

Table 2: Practical mixing parameters for common detergent products
Product Mixer speed Mixing time Temperature Key control point
Powdered washing detergent Ribbon: 20â40 rpm 10â15 min Ambient (25â35 Â°C) Avoid over-mixing (dust, segregation)
Liquid dishwash Propeller: 200â400 rpm 20â40 min 30â45 Â°C Control foaming during surfactant addition
Liquid laundry detergent High-shear: 1,000â3,000 rpm 30â60 min 40â60 Â°C Viscosity and pH stability
Emulsified / thickened cleaner Rotor-stator: 3,000â6,000 rpm 15â30 min 50â70 Â°C Emulsion stability, no phase separation

Source: Compiled from UNIDO (2010), Detergent Manufacturing Guide, and US EPA Safer Choice formulation guidance (public domain).

Temperature note: In hot African climates, ambient temperatures can already be 30â40 Â°C. You may need cooling, not heating, for some liquid products. Always measure the actual batch temperature, not the room temperature.

4. Homogenization and Emulsification

Homogenization reduces particle size and ensures uniform distribution. Emulsification combines oil and water phases into a stable mixture. For detergents, these operations matter most in liquid products â especially thickened cleaners, fabric softeners, and cream cleansers.

Use a rotor-stator or high-shear mixer for emulsification. Add the oil phase slowly to the water phase while mixing at high speed. Maintain temperature within 5 Â°C of the target. If the emulsion separates within 24 hours, your mixing speed, temperature, or emulsifier dosage is wrong. Test a small sample before scaling up.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Chemical Handling During Mixing

Detergent raw materials are hazardous. LABSA, SLES, caustic soda (NaOH), and soda ash cause severe skin burns and eye damage. Never add water to concentrated caustic soda â always add caustic to water slowly, as the reaction generates intense heat and can cause violent boiling and splashing. Wear chemical splash goggles, face shield, rubber gloves, apron, and closed shoes. Ensure adequate ventilation or local exhaust. Keep a running water source and eyewash station within 10 metres of the mixing area. In many African markets, PPE is the cheapest insurance you can buy â a single caustic splash injury can cost more than a year of PPE supplies.

5. Monitoring and Control of Mixing

You cannot control what you do not measure. At minimum, monitor and record the following for every batch:

  • Batch weight / volume â verify each ingredient by scale or flow meter.
  • Temperature â check at start, during addition, and at end.
  • pH â critical for liquid detergents; target 7â10 depending on product.
  • Viscosity â use a simple flow cup or Brookfield viscometer if available.
  • Appearance â colour, clarity, absence of lumps or separation.
  • Foam height â for dishwash and handwash, test with a standard shake test.

Keep a batch record sheet. In African SME operations, a simple paper log signed by the operator and supervisor is often enough for traceability and customer complaints. If you export or supply supermarkets, you may need digital records.

6. Cleaning and Changeover Procedures

Changeover between products â for example, from a bleach-based cleaner to a dishwash â must be thorough. Residues cause cross-contamination, off-odours, and quality failures. Follow this sequence:

  1. Drain and recover usable product residue where possible.
  2. Rinse with warm water (40â50 Â°C) to remove bulk product.
  3. Wash with detergent solution and brush all contact surfaces.
  4. Rinse with clean water until no foam remains.
  5. For bleach or caustic products, use a dilute acid rinse (e.g., citric acid) to neutralize residues.
  6. Inspect visually and by smell. If in doubt, clean again.
  7. Record the changeover in the cleaning log with date, time, operator, and products involved.

In hot, humid African conditions, wet surfaces grow bacteria and mould quickly. Dry equipment after cleaning where possible, and do not leave standing water in tanks overnight.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Verify all raw materials against the batch sheet before starting.
  • â Confirm mixer is clean and free from previous product residue.
  • â Check water quality â hardness affects surfactant performance.
  • â Add ingredients in the correct order; never dump all at once.
  • â Record speed, time, and temperature at each stage.
  • â Test pH, viscosity, and appearance before packaging.
  • â Wear full PPE â goggles, gloves, apron, closed shoes.
  • â Complete the batch record and cleaning log before signing off.

Further Reading

  • UNIDO â Detergent Manufacturing: A Guide for Small and Medium Enterprises (PDF)
  • US EPA Safer Choice â Cleaning Product Ingredient and Formulation Guidance
  • WHO â Chemical Safety in the Workplace (public health guidance)
  • ILO â Occupational Safety and Health in Chemical Handling
  • FAO â Small-Scale Processing Enterprise Development (relevant to SME operations)

Business-first summary: In African detergent manufacturing, mixing discipline is a profit centre, not a cost centre. Consistent mixing reduces rework, protects your brand, and lets you scale. Start simple, measure everything, train your operators, and keep safety first. Your mixing floor is where raw materials become money â treat it that way.

quiz.q: Which type of mixer is best for a small-scale detergent producer making 200 litres per day?
quiz.explanation: Batch mixing is simple and suitable for small volumes, while continuous and inline mixers are for larger or specialized operations.

quiz.q: What is an example of an inline mixer?
options: A) A paddle mixer in a drum
B) A static mixer in a pipe
quiz.explanation: A static mixer is placed inline in a pipe and has no moving parts, blending fluids as they flow.

quiz.q: Why is continuous mixing not recommended for beginners?
options: B) It requires expensive equipment and controls
C) It only works for powders
quiz.explanation: Continuous mixing needs pumps, flow meters, and automatic controls, which are costly and complex for small businesses.

quiz.q: When making liquid detergent, what should you add first?
quiz.explanation: Water is the base and should be added first, then other ingredients are added in order of difficulty to dissolve.

quiz.q: Why should you never add water to concentrated acid?
options: A) It causes a violent reaction
B) It makes the acid weaker
C) It creates too much foam
quiz.explanation: Adding water to acid can cause a violent exothermic reaction; always add acid to water slowly.

quiz.q: In what order should you add fragrance and colour?
options: B) After neutralisation but before salt
C) Last, after the mixture has cooled below 40Â°C
quiz.explanation: Fragrance and colour are heat-sensitive, so they should be added last when the mixture is cool.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mixing speed for dissolving powders in water?
quiz.explanation: Medium speed (300-600 RPM) effectively dissolves powders without creating excessive foam.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing too fast when dissolving powders?
options: B) It creates foam and air bubbles
quiz.explanation: High speed introduces air, leading to foam that is hard to remove and can affect product quality.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended temperature during neutralisation of liquid detergent?
quiz.explanation: Keeping the temperature below 60Â°C prevents fragrance evaporation and colour fading.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of emulsification in detergent making?
options: A) To make the product thicker
B) To mix oil and water permanently
quiz.explanation: Emulsification blends oil and water into a stable mixture that does not separate.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common emulsifier used in detergents?
quiz.explanation: Alcohol ethoxylates are nonionic surfactants that help stabilize emulsions.

quiz.q: What is homogenization?
options: B) Forcing mixture through a narrow gap at high pressure
quiz.explanation: Homogenization reduces oil droplet size by forcing the mixture through a small opening under high pressure.

quiz.q: Why should salt not be added before emulsification?
options: A) It makes the emulsion too thick
B) It can break the emulsion
D) It reacts with the emulsifier
quiz.explanation: Salt can destabilize the emulsion, so it should be added after the emulsion is formed and cooled.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for emulsion stability?
options: B) Leave a sample in a bottle for 7 days
quiz.explanation: Observing separation over a week indicates if the emulsion is stable.

quiz.q: What should you monitor during mixing to ensure quality?
quiz.explanation: pH, viscosity, and temperature are key parameters that affect product quality and stability.

quiz.q: What is the acceptable pH range for most liquid detergents?
quiz.explanation: Most liquid detergents are formulated to be near neutral to slightly alkaline, pH 7-9.

quiz.q: If the viscosity of your liquid detergent is too low, what should you add?
quiz.explanation: Adding a small amount of salt solution thickens the detergent by increasing micelle formation.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record mixing parameters for every batch?
options: B) To repeat good results and trace problems
quiz.explanation: Records help you replicate successful batches and identify causes of defects.

quiz.q: What should you do if the pH of your batch is too high?
quiz.explanation: Adding acid neutralizes excess alkali, lowering the pH.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning a mixing tank after a batch?
quiz.explanation: Draining leftover product prevents contamination and makes cleaning easier.

quiz.q: Which cleaning agent is effective for removing oily residues?
quiz.explanation: Detergent solution breaks down oils and greases effectively.

quiz.q: Why is it important to neutralize with a weak acid after caustic cleaning?
options: A) To remove any caustic residue
quiz.explanation: Neutralizing ensures no caustic remains, which could affect the next batch's pH.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to save water during cleaning?
options: B) Use a hose with free flow
C) Fill the tank and dump
quiz.explanation: High-pressure sprayers use less water and are more effective at removing residues.

quiz.q: What does 'changeover' mean in detergent production?
options: A) Switching from one product to another
quiz.explanation: Changeover refers to the process of cleaning and preparing equipment to make a different product.

quiz.q: What should you check before starting a new batch after changeover?
options: A) The last rinse water pH is neutral
D) The colour of the tank
quiz.explanation: Checking that the rinse water is neutral ensures no cleaning chemicals remain.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean immediately after each batch?
options: A) Dried detergent is harder to remove
quiz.explanation: Immediate cleaning prevents hardening, saves time, and maintains hygiene.

quiz.q: What is a static mixer?
options: A) A mixer with moving blades
B) A pipe with twisted blades inside
quiz.explanation: A static mixer has no moving parts; it uses internal baffles to blend fluids as they flow.

quiz.q: For a 200-litre batch of liquid dishwash, how much water should you start with?
quiz.explanation: Starting with about 70-75% of the final volume (150 litres) leaves room for other ingredients.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding salt to liquid detergent?
quiz.explanation: Salt increases viscosity by promoting micelle formation, thickening the product.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a stable emulsion?
options: B) It remains uniform for 7 days
quiz.explanation: Stable emulsions do not separate over time; a week-long test is a good indicator.
